threads_text: Google just announced Gemini 4 Carbon, and it took the top spot on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with 59, one point ahead of Claude Opus 5.5. The catch: only a small group of cyber defenders can use it for now, and Google gave no date for everyone else. Should AI labs hold back their strongest models like this?
caption:
Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28, its strongest model so far.
It scored 59 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, first place, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 at 58.
For now only selected cyber defenders get access. Developers and consumers get it later, with no date yet.

Should the most powerful AI models be held back from the public?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

paragraphs.text: Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28, 2026, describing it as its strongest model so far, with leading cybersecurity and long horizon abilities. The announcement was written by Koray Kavukcuoglu, senior vice president at Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google. Carbon builds on Gemini 4 Argon, which Google launched two weeks earlier.

According to Google, Carbon ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0 with a score of 59. VentureBeat reported that Claude Opus 5.5 scored 58 on the same index, GPT-6 Astra scored 57 and Argon scored 50. Artificial Analysis says 60 percent of the v5 index relies on private tests or withheld answers.
A model aimed at security work

Google is presenting Carbon chiefly as a security model. On SEC-bench Pro, which measures finding vulnerabilities, it scored 88.2 percent, up from 83.4 percent for Argon. On ExploitGym, an exploitation test, it reached 54.8 percent, compared with 42.0 percent for Argon. On CWE-bench, a patching test, it scored 71.0 percent. Google said these external evaluations were run without guardrails.

The company also said its Chrome team found Carbon more than ten times better than another lab's large frontier model at generating high quality patches, and that the cloud security firm Wiz saw it lead on web penetration testing benchmarks. VentureBeat noted that Google did not publish the underlying results for the Chrome comparison. Internally, Google reported more than double Argon's success rate at writing secure code.

Google said the model is designed for long, multi step engineering jobs such as tracing and fixing subtle bugs in large codebases, and that internal teams have seen it run for days. On WebDev Arena it gained 89 Elo points to reach fourth place at 1769.

Access is restricted at launch. Starting the week of the announcement, Google is giving Carbon to a subset of cyber defenders and plans to add trusted partners gradually through its Fairwind Program. Developers, businesses and consumers will get it through Google's products as soon as possible, the company said, while it keeps refining guardrails. No date was given. Google also said it is taking part in the United States government's voluntary pre release model testing.

The introductory price matches Argon: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with a 95 percent discount on cached input. After the introductory period, the price rises to $4 and $20. VentureBeat reported that Artificial Analysis lists Carbon as having no publicly available API yet.

Carbon does not lead every test. In Google's own comparison, GPT-6 Astra scored 65.5 percent on FrontierSWE 2 against Carbon's 61.2 percent, and Claude Opus 5.5 scored 87.2 percent on an offline subset of OSWorld 2.1 against 81.5 percent. On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Claude Code with Opus 5.5 led at 62, while Carbon scored 59. VentureBeat also reported that Carbon's hallucination rate on AA-Omniscience was 11 percent, compared with 4 percent for Argon, even as its share of correct answers rose to 58 percent from 48 percent.

On safety, Google said Carbon uses the same layered approach as Argon, including training, real time misuse defenses, prompt injection resilience and chain of thought monitoring. It reported a 0.0 percent attack success rate on Gray Swan's indirect prompt injection benchmark and said high severity misalignment alerts in internal coding environments fell by almost 80 percent.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the release shows how the top of the model race now turns on single points, with Google, Anthropic and OpenAI separated by a narrow margin on the main index. Holding back a model built for exploitation and patching also follows a pattern of labs giving security focused systems to defenders before the general public.
The next step to watch is when Google opens Carbon beyond the Fairwind Program, and whether its index lead holds once outside developers can test it directly.
